message.content:
When Nicolaus Copernicus formulated his heliocentric theory in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, Europe was shifting from medieval scholasticism toward Renaissance humanism.
Politically, the continent was fragmented among the Habsburgs, Valois, Ottomans, and papal states, while the Protestant Reformation strained Catholic unity and local power.
In Poland-Lithuania relative tolerance and royal weakness gave Copernicus room as canon of Warmia, yet the Church still guarded astronomical doctrine.
The resulting cactiform climate of religious scrutiny, imperial rivalry, and intellectual renewal made his model dangerous, novel, and politically inconvenient.
